clinicalScope: Envenoming from venomous snake bites in humans presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Snake Bite Envenoming
subject: Surgery
summary: Snake bite envenoming is a common emergency in rural East Africa, often caused by vipers (cytotoxic/haemorrhagic) or cobras (neurotoxic). Prompt first‑aid, recognition of systemic signs, and antivenom are the cornerstones of care.

sections.p: Envenoming occurs when venom is injected into the victim’s tissue, producing local and/or systemic effects. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by bedside clotting tests.
b: History of bite, time, and snake identification if possible
Visible fang marks or puncture wounds
Progressive swelling, pain, or systemic signs

sections.p: Severity is graded by the presence of local tissue injury, systemic neuro‑ or haemotoxic signs, and laboratory coagulopathy.
b: Mild: local pain, minimal swelling, no systemic signs
Moderate: expanding oedema, early neuro‑signs, abnormal 20‑WBCT
Severe: neuro‑paralysis, severe coagulopathy, renal failure, shock

sections.p: In East Africa the two main venom types are cytotoxic/haemorrhagic (viperidae) and neurotoxic (elapidae).
b: Viper bites (e.g., Puff‑adder, Bitis arietans) – cytotoxic, cause tissue necrosis and coagulopathy
Cobra bites (Naja spp.) – neurotoxic, cause descending paralysis
Mambas and other elapids – primarily neurotoxic
Rarely, non‑venomous bites or dry bites

sections.p: Presentation evolves from the bite site outward, then systemically if venom spreads.
b: Local: pain, swelling, bruising, blistering, necrosis
Haemotoxic: bleeding gums, ecchymoses, prolonged clotting, haematuria
Neurotoxic: ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, descending flaccid paralysis
Renal: oliguria, rising creatinine, dark urine

sections.p: Investigations guide severity assessment and monitor complications; many are feasible in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects venom‑induced coagulopathy; un‑clotted blood after 20 min indicates systemic haemotoxicity
Shows anaemia, leukocytosis, platelet trends; falling platelets suggest consumptive coagulopathy
Monitors acute kidney injury; rising creatinine signals renal involvement
Quantifies coagulation defect; prolonged PT/INR confirms systemic coagulopathy
Tracks progression of neuro‑toxicity; worsening bulbar signs demand airway protection

sections.p: Complications may develop hours to days after the bite and can be fatal if missed.
b: Airway compromise from neuro‑paralysis
Severe coagulopathy with uncontrolled bleeding
Compartment syndrome after massive swelling
Acute kidney injury from haemoglobinuria or direct nephrotoxicity
Secondary infection of necrotic tissue

sections.p: Management follows ABCs, early antivenom, and targeted supportive care.
b: Immobilise the limb with a splint; keep at heart level; reassure patient
Give antivenom as soon as systemic signs appear or 20‑WBCT is abnormal; repeat doses until clinical improvement
Treat coagulopathy primarily with antivenom; give fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate only if bleeding persists after antivenom
Provide analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and wound care; consider antibiotics for secondary infection
Monitor airway; intubate early if bulbar signs progress
Correct hypotension with crystalloid bolus; avoid excessive fluids if renal failure suspected

sections.p: After the acute phase, watch for delayed toxicity and educate on avoidance.
b: Re‑assess limb swelling, neuro‑signs, and coagulation every 6–12 h for at least 48 h
Monitor renal function daily for 5 days; intervene early for AKI
Educate on wearing protective boots, using torches at night, and safe snake‑handling practices
Encourage community awareness of local venomous species and prompt transport to health facilities
Cellulitis – lacks rapid progression, systemic neuro‑signs, and abnormal 20‑WBCT
Deep vein thrombosis – presents with unilateral swelling but no bite mark or coagulopathy
Acute compartment syndrome from trauma – no venom‑induced coagulopathy; antivenom is unnecessary

sections.p: Certain bedside tests may give false reassurance.
b: A normal 20‑WBCT early after bite does not rule out delayed haemotoxicity; repeat after 30 min if suspicion remains
Platelet count may be normal initially despite evolving consumptive coagulopathy

whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled bleeding or rapidly falling haemoglobin
Signs of compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, tense swelling)

faq.q: What is the first step after a snake bite?
faq.a: Immobilise the bitten limb, reassure the patient, remove tight clothing or jewellery, and arrange rapid transport while maintaining ABCs.
Continue antivenom until clinical signs of envenoming (e.g., swelling, neuro‑signs, abnormal 20‑WBCT) improve and coagulation normalises; then no further doses are needed.

faq.q: Why is fresh frozen plasma not the primary treatment for venom‑induced coagulopathy?
faq.a: Antivenom neutralises the venom causing the coagulopathy; blood products only support bleeding and are used if haemorrhage persists after antivenom.

exam: A farmer presents 2 h after a puff‑adder bite with rapidly expanding leg swelling and a prolonged 20‑WBCT. What is the next best step? — Administer antivenom immediately; monitor coagulation and limb swelling.

How does neuro‑toxic envenoming differ from cytotoxic envenoming on examination? — Neuro‑toxic shows descending paralysis, ptosis, and respiratory muscle weakness; cytotoxic shows intense local swelling, bruising, and coagulopathy.
Why is the 20‑minute whole blood clotting test essential in low‑resource settings? — It detects systemic haemotoxicity without laboratory equipment, guiding antivenom use.

A patient develops tense calf swelling 12 h after a viper bite but has normal coagulation after antivenom. What should you consider? — Compartment syndrome; measure compartment pressure and consider fasciotomy only after correcting any residual coagulopathy.
What are the contraindications to giving antivenom in a snake‑bite patient? — Known severe IgE‑mediated allergy to antivenom; otherwise, clinical signs dictate use.
Explain why tetanus prophylaxis is given to all snake‑bite victims. — Bite wounds are contaminated; tetanus risk is high in rural settings, and prophylaxis prevents a potentially fatal infection.

A child presents with a dry bite (no signs of envenoming). What is the appropriate management? — Observe for at least 24 h, immobilise limb, educate caregivers; antivenom is not indicated without systemic signs.

Which laboratory test is least useful for immediate decision‑making in a low‑resource snake‑bite setting? — Serum creatinine; while important for AKI monitoring, it does not guide acute antivenom administration.
